title: When Did Sirens Become Mermaids?
subtitle: Homer's voices without bodies, Greek birds with women's faces, a Latin book of monsters, and the centuries when wings and fish tails shared one name

segments.text: When did sirens become mermaids? Today, the word siren often brings to mind a woman with the tail of a fish, singing sailors to their doom. The French word for a mermaid is sirène. In Italian and Spanish, it is sirena. But the oldest pictures of sirens show something else. They have wings, and the feet of birds.

The story begins with Homer. In the twelfth book of the Odyssey, the goddess Circe warns Odysseus. The Sirens sit in a meadow, she says, and around them lies a great heap of bones. Whoever hears their song never returns home. So Odysseus plugs his men's ears with wax, and they tie him to the mast. Homer speaks of only two Sirens, and he tells us what they sing. They know, they say, everything that happened at Troy. But he never tells us what they look like. He gives them a voice, and nothing more.

Greek artists filled in the rest. By the seventh century before Christ, they were making sirens with the heads of women and the bodies of birds. They appear on painted vases, on perfume flasks, and as small figures in clay and bronze.
Not every early siren was a woman. On this perfume vessel from Boeotia, made in the middle of the sixth century before Christ, a siren has a pointed beard.

Greek poets describe the same shape. In a play by Euripides, first staged in four twelve before Christ, Helen calls on the Sirens as winged maidens, daughters of the Earth. In the third century before Christ, Apollonius of Rhodes writes that they looked partly like birds, and partly like maidens.

Why would singers by the sea have wings? The Roman poet Ovid answers with a story. The Sirens, he writes, were companions of Persephone. When she was carried away, they searched the whole earth for her. So that they could search across the sea as well, they wished for wings. The gods agreed, and their limbs turned golden with feathers. But they kept the faces of girls, and their human voices.

Modern scholars have suggested other answers. In Egypt, the soul of a dead person could be shown as a bird with a human head. The Egyptian ba-bird is one proposed model for the Greek siren. Greek artists also placed sirens on tombs, as mourners. From early Greek art to the seventh century after Christ, the bird-shaped siren appears in sources more than a thousand years apart.

The change appears in a strange little book, written in Latin, probably in England, around the year seven hundred. It is called the Book of Monsters. Its author describes the sirens as sea girls, who deceive sailors with their beauty and their song. From the head to the navel, he writes, they have the body of a maiden. But they have the scaly tails of fish, and with them they always hide in the deep.

This is one of the earliest surviving Latin descriptions to give sirens the tails of fish. The author does not say where he found the idea. In the centuries that followed, fish-tailed women spread through medieval art, even into books of coats of arms.

Yet the birds did not vanish. In the early six hundreds, Isidore of Seville had written in his great encyclopedia that the sirens were part maidens, part birds, with wings and claws. Medieval books of beasts copied his words for centuries, even as their painters drew fish tails. And one medieval text gives sirens both the hooked claws of an eagle, and the scaly tails of fish.
In these books, the siren became a lesson. Some compare her song to the pleasures of the world. The sailors fall asleep to the music, and the sirens attack them.

So, when did sirens become mermaids? Homer gave them a song, but no body. Greek artists and poets gave them wings. One of the earliest fish tails is in a Latin book from around the year seven hundred. For centuries after that, wings and fish tails shared the same name.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, the shape changes, and the song stays the same.
